R06-C-01: Few scientific failures are held against a discipline as often as seismology's inability to say when the next large earthquake will strike. The public imagines that a sufficiently clever instrument, placed in the right fault zone, ought eventually to detect a warning sign, much as a barometer falls before a storm. Over the past century researchers have pursued many such signs, from changes in groundwater levels and gas emissions to swarms of small tremors and odd animal behaviour. Each has, at one time or another, appeared to precede a particular earthquake, and each has failed when tested against the many earthquakes that came without it and the many apparent warnings that were followed by nothing. It is worth separating two activities that ordinary speech runs together. A prediction, in the sense the public wants, names a place, a magnitude and a narrow window of time: a strong earthquake near this town within the next week. A forecast states a probability over a longer period: a given chance of shaking above some level in this region within the next thirty years. The first remains beyond reach, and many seismologists suspect it may stay there, because whether a small rupture grows into a large one seems to depend on conditions deep in the crust that no instrument can survey in detail. The second is routine, and it is far from useless. Forecasts are what building codes are written from. When engineers decide how strongly a hospital must be braced, or which soils are too loose to build on, they are acting on probabilities of exactly this kind. A city that has absorbed its long-term hazard into the way it builds has, in effect, already received the most valuable warning seismology can give, though nobody experiences it as a warning, since it arrives years before the event and asks for money rather than flight. The objection that a probability is too vague to act on mistakes the kind of decision at stake. Few people would evacuate a city on the strength of a one-in-twenty chance spread over three decades, and nobody should. But a decision about whether to reinforce a school is not a decision about this week; it is a decision about the lifetime of a building, and over that lifetime a one-in-twenty chance is large. This does not mean that the search for warning signs should be abandoned, since a reliable one would save lives that codes cannot. It means that the discipline should not be judged by its failure at a task it may never accomplish while its success at a quieter task goes unremarked.
R06-C-02: For much of the twentieth century, weather forecasting was imagined as a problem of insufficient detail. If the atmosphere obeyed known physical laws, then better observations and faster calculation should, in principle, allow the future to be computed as far ahead as anyone liked. The recognition that the atmosphere is chaotic, in the technical sense that tiny differences in its starting state grow until they dominate the outcome, seemed at first to end that hope. Beyond a horizon of a week or two, no conceivable improvement in measurement would make a single calculated forecast reliable, because no measurement can be perfect and every imperfection is eventually amplified. What is striking is how the discipline turned this limit into a method. Instead of running a model once from the best available estimate of the present, forecasting centres now run it dozens of times, each from a starting state nudged slightly within the range of what observations allow. If the runs stay close together, the atmosphere is in a predictable mood and the forecast can be stated with confidence; if they fan out, the spread itself is the information, telling forecasters that several quite different outcomes remain live. Chaos, which looked like a verdict against prediction, became a way of measuring how much prediction a given situation permits. Much of this gain is lost in the last step, when forecasts reach the public. A phone application that shows a single icon for Thursday, a cloud with three raindrops, has quietly discarded the ensemble and kept only something like its average. Users then judge the forecast by whether it rained, and a forecast that correctly said the outcome was uncertain is remembered as a forecast that was wrong. The habit is understandable, since most people want a decision rather than a distribution, but it trains the public to expect a kind of certainty the science has explicitly given up. It would be a mistake, however, to treat the ensemble as a perfectly honest witness. Every run in it uses the same model, with the same simplified treatment of clouds, mountains and ocean surfaces, so errors built into the model are shared by all the members and do not show up as spread. An ensemble can therefore agree with itself and still be wrong, and forecasters spend considerable effort checking whether its spread matches the errors actually observed over many past forecasts. The spread is a measure of uncertainty, not a guarantee of it, and its value depends on that continual comparison with what the weather in fact did.
R06-C-03: Among the records of past climate, ice cores enjoy a special prestige. Drilled from the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, they contain small bubbles of air sealed off as snow was buried and compressed, so that a scientist can, in a sense, hold in a laboratory a sample of the atmosphere as it was long before any human being farmed. Tree rings, lake sediments and the shells of tiny marine organisms all have to be translated into climate through some chain of reasoning. The bubbles in ice seem to need no translation at all: the gas is simply there, waiting to be measured. The appearance of directness is partly an illusion, and an instructive one. Snow does not seal itself the moment it falls. For decades, centuries or, at the driest sites, far longer, depending on how quickly snow accumulates, the upper layer remains porous, and air from the surface continues to mix downward through it. By the time the bubbles finally close, the gas they hold is considerably younger than the ice that surrounds it. To date the air, then, researchers must model how compaction proceeds at a given site, which in turn depends on temperature and snowfall, the very quantities the core is being used to reconstruct. Temperature itself is not read off the ice but inferred from the proportions of heavier and lighter forms of water, a relationship calibrated against modern observations and assumed to have held in the past. None of this makes the records untrustworthy. It does, however, change where their authority comes from. A core is persuasive not because it bypasses interpretation but because its interpretations can be checked against one another and against independent archives. Traces of very large volcanic eruptions, which can appear in cores drilled at opposite ends of the planet, allow records to be aligned; the timing of changes in ice can be compared with changes recorded in ocean sediments, whose dating rests on quite different assumptions. When such independent lines agree, the agreement is far harder to explain away than any single measurement, however direct it seems. The point matters beyond the laboratory. Public arguments about climate often treat evidence as either raw and therefore reliable or interpreted and therefore suspect. Ice cores show why this division is unhelpful. Almost all scientific evidence is interpreted; what distinguishes strong evidence from weak is whether its interpretations are exposed to independent tests that could have failed. A measurement trusted because it seemed to speak for itself would deserve less confidence than one whose inferences had been stated openly and checked.
R06-C-04: When the sea threatens a coastal town, the first response is almost always to defend it. Walls are raised, beaches are replenished with sand pumped from offshore, and the line between land and water is held where it has always been. To propose instead that some places should be gradually abandoned sounds like defeatism, a confession that the town has been given up for lost. Yet the choice is rarely between holding the line and surrendering it. More often it is between retreat that is planned and retreat that is forced. Defences are not permanent solutions but commitments that grow. A wall built to withstand the storms of today must be raised as the sea rises, and every raising protects more property that was built because the previous wall made it seem safe. Each round of investment makes the next one harder to refuse, since abandoning the wall would now mean abandoning more. Engineers can usually design a higher barrier; the deeper difficulty is that the community sheltering behind it has, by then, organised its entire economic life around the expectation that the barrier will hold. In low-lying places the expense eventually outruns what the community can pay, and the decision to leave is then made not by a council in calm weather but by the storm that finally breaks through. Retreat imposed in that way is the worst version of a policy that might have been tolerable. Households leave in a rush, with property that has lost its value overnight, and they scatter wherever they can find housing, so that the neighbourhood that made the place worth defending dissolves. Planned retreat, by contrast, can be slow. A town can stop permitting new building in the most exposed areas, offer to buy homes when owners choose to sell, and move a school or a clinic inland when it would have needed rebuilding anyway. Spread over decades, such steps let a community move as a community. None of this means that every shore should be abandoned. Some coasts carry so much population and infrastructure that defending them is plainly worth the cost, and in poor places the money for orderly relocation is often lacking. Nor can retreat simply be ordered from above; people who have lived beside the water for generations have reasons for staying that no compensation formula captures, and a plan that ignores them will fail. The argument is narrower: retreat belongs among the options from the start, weighed openly alongside walls, rather than held back as an admission of failure until it can no longer be chosen at all.
R06-C-05: Each summer, the arrival of the monsoon over the southern tip of the Indian peninsula is announced on a particular day, and the date is reported as if something had been observed to happen: the rains have come. Newspapers compare it with the long-term average, and a delay of a week becomes a story about anxious farmers and rising food prices. Behind the announcement, however, lies not an event but a decision. The monsoon has no sharp leading edge. Showers build over days or weeks, winds shift gradually, and early bursts of rain may be followed by long dry spells. To fix a single day, forecasters must apply criteria, thresholds of rainfall across a set of stations and of wind and cloud, chosen so that the date can be determined consistently from one year to the next. Calling the onset a convention is not to call it arbitrary. Good criteria pick out a real change in the behaviour of the atmosphere, and fixing them in advance prevents the date from being adjusted to suit hopes or headlines. A consistent definition also makes years comparable, so that researchers can ask whether onsets have tended to come earlier or later over many decades. Conventions of this kind are the ordinary machinery of science; the point at which a heavy shower counts as an extreme rainfall event, or a tropical storm as a cyclone, is fixed in the same way. The trouble begins when the convention is mistaken for the thing it marks. A declared onset tells a farmer that a threshold was crossed somewhere along the coast; it does not tell her whether the soil in her own district holds enough moisture for seed to survive the next fortnight. In some years the rains, having satisfied the criteria, stall for weeks, and farmers who sowed on the strength of the announcement watch their seedlings wither. The date did nothing wrong; it was simply asked to answer a question it was never designed to answer. The lesson is not that the onset date should be abolished, since it serves research and public communication reasonably well, but that a single number cannot serve every purpose at once. A measure built for comparing years across a century need not be the measure that should guide a decision about sowing next week. Agricultural advice would be better anchored in local indicators, such as accumulated rainfall and soil moisture in the district concerned, with the national date treated as background rather than as a signal to act. Definitions in climate science, like definitions elsewhere, should be judged by whether they fit the decision they are used to inform.
R06-C-06: Among researchers who study catastrophes, a slogan has become something close to a creed: there is no such thing as a natural disaster. The claim is not that earthquakes, floods and cyclones are human inventions. It is that a hazard, a physical event of a certain size, becomes a disaster only when it meets people and structures unable to withstand it. A cyclone that crosses an empty coastline is a fact about the atmosphere; the same cyclone striking a crowded delta of unreinforced houses with no warning system is a social event, and the scale of its damage is decided as much by the delta's history as by the storm. The slogan earns its popularity because it redirects attention to what can be changed. Two cities shaken by earthquakes of similar strength may suffer wholly different losses, one counting broken windows and the other thousands of dead, and the difference lies in building standards, in whether they were enforced, in where the poor were permitted or forced to live. Calling the outcome natural lets those decisions disappear from view. It encourages the belief that loss is fate, and fate calls for sympathy after the event rather than investment before it. Taken literally, however, the slogan claims too much. Some events are large enough that no plausible arrangement of society would have prevented great loss: a sufficiently large eruption, or a wave of extraordinary height arriving within minutes, can overwhelm even well-prepared places. To insist that every such loss was socially produced is to imply that someone could have prevented it, which may be false, and in its cruder versions comes close to suggesting that the people harmed were responsible for their own exposure. The slogan can also tempt its users to neglect the physical science of hazards, as though knowing how often floods of a given size recur mattered less than studying the societies they strike, when the two kinds of knowledge are needed together. The insight is worth keeping and the absolutism worth dropping. A more defensible claim is that the size of a disaster is never simply natural: the hazard sets the challenge, but how much of the challenge becomes catastrophe depends on choices made long before. This version keeps the slogan's critical edge, its refusal to let preventable deaths be filed under bad luck, while admitting that nature sometimes sets challenges that no society could fully meet.
R06-C-07: Geologists divide the history of the Earth into named intervals, and they are unusually strict about where one interval ends and the next begins. A boundary is not fixed by a date written in a textbook but by a physical reference point: a particular layer in a particular sequence of rock or sediment, chosen because it records a change that can be recognised in deposits across the globe, and marked, in the profession's half-joking phrase, by a golden spike. The rigour has a purpose. The time scale exists so that a geologist examining strata on one continent can say with confidence that they formed at the same time as strata on another, and a boundary that cannot be traced from place to place is of little use for that task. Precision about where a boundary lies is, in this sense, the price paid for precision about when. The proposal that we now live in a new interval, the Anthropocene, defined by the imprint of human activity on the planet, has therefore been argued in unusual terms. Much of the debate has concerned not whether humans have transformed the Earth, a point few specialists now dispute, but where the spike should go. Candidates have ranged from the spread of farming thousands of years ago, through the industrial burning of coal, to the middle of the twentieth century, when fallout from nuclear weapons tests left a thin but nearly worldwide trace in sediments and ice. The later dates are favoured partly because they are sharp. A signal laid down within a few years everywhere is exactly what a stratigrapher wants; the slow spread of farming, which reached different regions in different millennia, is not. Here the demands of the time scale begin to distort the story they are meant to record. Human influence on the Earth did not arrive at one moment. Forests were cleared, soils eroded and large animals hunted to extinction over thousands of years, at different times on different continents, and the acceleration of the last century was the culmination of that history rather than its beginning. Choosing the mid-twentieth century because its markers are crisp risks implying that the transformation began then, and that everything before it belongs to an untouched natural world. A boundary drawn there would be accurate about the rocks and misleading about the long human history that produced them. The criterion that makes a boundary useful for correlating rocks is not the criterion that makes it faithful to a process that was, by its nature, gradual and uneven. None of this shows that formal definition is pointless. A ratified boundary would give researchers in many fields a common reference, and it would carry an authority that informal usage lacks. Some defenders of formalisation fear that without it the idea will remain a slogan, borrowed by commentators and never disciplined by evidence. But the concept does not need a spike to do its intellectual work. The claim that human activity has become a force comparable to the processes that build mountains and shift climates rests on measurements of carbon, sediment, species and nitrogen, and those measurements remain what they are whatever any committee decides. A concept can be rigorous without being a unit of the time scale; geologists already speak, informally, of great events that unfolded over long and varying spans. The Anthropocene may be better understood in that way, as a transformation with a long and diachronous history, rather than as an epoch that began in a particular year.
R06-C-08: The founders of modern geology won their central argument so completely that its terms are now remembered mainly as a caricature. Against older accounts that explained mountains, valleys and buried shells by a few vast upheavals, they proposed that the Earth's features had been shaped by the same slow processes that can be watched today: rivers cutting their beds, waves wearing down cliffs, sediment settling grain by grain on the floors of lakes and seas. Given enough time, such ordinary causes could account for extraordinary results, and the immense age of the Earth that this view required became one of its most consequential implications. The doctrine came to be called uniformitarianism, and its rival, the appeal to sudden and violent change, catastrophism. In the familiar telling, patient observation defeated speculation. The telling is unfair to both sides. Uniformitarianism bundled together several claims of very different standing. One was that the laws of nature have not changed, so that water flowed and rock fractured in the past as it does now. Another was methodological: that a geologist should first try to explain the record by causes known to operate, and invoke unobserved ones only when those fail. A third was a claim about the Earth itself, that change had generally proceeded at gentle and roughly steady rates. The first two are close to the preconditions of any historical science. The third is an empirical hypothesis, and it could have turned out false. In part, it did. Through much of the twentieth century, geologists who proposed sudden events of enormous scale met resistance out of proportion to their evidence. A landscape of deep channels and giant ripples in the north-western United States was long attributed to ordinary erosion before it was accepted as the work of floods released when ice dams failed; the suggestion that the mass extinction at the end of the age of dinosaurs followed the impact of a large asteroid met at first with widespread doubt, some of it dismissive. In both cases the objection was less that the evidence was weak than that the explanation sounded like the discredited catastrophism of the past. A rule of method, prefer known causes, had hardened into a belief about what the Earth was permitted to have done. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the old suspicion of catastrophes was mere prejudice. Many early catastrophist explanations could not be tested: they posited events of unspecified cause that left no trace except the very features they were invoked to explain. Against such accounts, a demand for known causes was a reasonable discipline, and it is part of why the later catastrophes were eventually accepted. The flood hypothesis prevailed when the lake held back by the ice and the shorelines it left were identified; the impact hypothesis prevailed when a thin layer rich in a rare metal was traced around the world and a buried crater of the right age was found. What persuaded geologists was not a relaxation of the old standard but evidence that met it. The view that now prevails keeps the uniformity of laws and the preference for testable causes while abandoning the assumption of uniform rates. The Earth's history includes long stretches of slow change punctuated by rare events of great violence, and both are explained by the same physics; neither the slow nor the violent is an exception that must apologise for itself. The lesson reaches beyond geology. A principle adopted to keep inquiry honest can, if it is mistaken for a description of the world, end by closing questions it was meant to keep open.
